title: Apuleius Tried for Magic at Sabratha; Acquitted
description: Around 158 CE, Apuleius of Madauros was tried before the proconsul Claudius Maximus at Sabratha on charges of practicing magic (veneficium) — specifically, that he had used magical means to persuade the widow Pudentilla to marry him. Apuleius defended himself with the Apologia (also known as De Magia), a sophisticated rhetorical defense that distinguished philosophical natural magic from criminal veneficium and argued that his accusers were motivated by financial interest. He was acquitted. The Apologia is the only surviving first-person defense against ancient magic charges and constitutes an invaluable source for understanding Roman legal and social attitudes toward magic.
historiographical_note: The Apologia has been extensively analyzed by Christopher Jones, Kimberly Stratton, and Vincent Hunink as evidence for Roman legal procedures in magic trials and the rhetorical strategies available to defendants, making it uniquely valuable for comparative legal history.
source_method: Published scholarship; Apuleius Apologia; secondary classical scholarship
